source_text: Verum imbecillum caecae opinionis patrocinium multiplicat peccata, non minuit. Hic igitur miserorum pruritus et sponte aegrescentium, nullum contra ipsam rationem valebit pondus afferre; sed quia nonnullis Scripturarum locis, et maxime apostoli Pauli sermonibus confirmari asserunt naturale peccatum, quorum expositionem in secundum volumen distuli, eiusque reddendae tempus est; breviter prius (ut fiat lector instructior), et quae sint acta, et quae sint agenda distinguam. Ostensum est ergo, nihil posse per sanctas Scripturas probari, quod iustitia non possit tueri; quia si in lege Dei est perfecta forma iustitiae, nihil per eam adversaria eius, id est, iniustitia sinitur virtutis acquirere; ac per hoc, quod ratio arguit, non potest auctoritas vindicare. Deinde probatum est, Deum nobis notum esse virtutibus; huius ergo iustitiam ut omnipotentiam confitendam; cuius si admittatur excidium, maiestas incipiet tota nutare; quia ita Deus iustus est, ut si probaretur iustus non esse, convinceretur Deus non esse; conclusumque est, nos Deum aequissimum in Trinitate venerari; et irrefutabiliter apparuit, non posse ab eo peccatum alienum parvulis imputari.
pass_a_gloss: But the weak patronage of a blind opinion multiplies sins, it does not lessen them. This itch, therefore, of the wretched and of those growing sick of their own accord will be able to bring no weight against reason itself; but because they assert that natural sin is confirmed by some places of the Scriptures, and especially by the speeches of the apostle Paul, whose exposition I postponed into the second volume, and the time of rendering it is here; first briefly (that the reader may be made more instructed) I will distinguish both what things have been done and what things are to be done. It has been shown, therefore, that nothing can be proved through the holy Scriptures which justice cannot guard; because if in the law of God there is the perfect form of justice, nothing through it is allowed to its adversary, that is injustice, to acquire of virtue; and through this, what reason convicts, authority cannot vindicate. Next it has been proved that God is known to us by virtues; that his justice, therefore, is to be confessed as his omnipotence; if the destruction of which is admitted, the whole majesty will begin to totter; because God is just in such a way that if he were proved not to be just, he would be convicted not to be God; and it has been concluded that we venerate a most equitable God in the Trinity; and it has irrefutably appeared that another's sin cannot be imputed by him to little children.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS parvulus; Blaise infants in original-sin debate

pass_b_english: But the feeble protection offered by blind opinion increases sins; it does not diminish them. This itch of miserable people who willingly make themselves sick will carry no weight against reason itself. Yet they claim that certain scriptural passages, especially the words of the apostle Paul, establish natural sin. I postponed explaining those passages until the second book, and now it is time to fulfill that promise. First, to equip the reader better, I will briefly distinguish what has been done from what remains. We have shown that nothing can be proved from holy Scripture which justice cannot uphold. If God’s law contains justice in its perfect form, then its adversary, injustice, can gain no strength through that law. Consequently, authority cannot defend what reason disproves. Next we proved that God is known to us by his virtues. We must therefore confess his justice just as we confess his almighty power. If his justice is allowed to collapse, his whole majesty will begin to totter. God is just in such a way that, if he were proved unjust, he would be proved not to be God. We concluded that we worship God in the Trinity as perfectly just, and it became irrefutably clear that he cannot charge infants with someone else’s sin.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
